I suspect the on-load tap changer on Transformer 1 at site MAIN is wearing. I'd like to know whether it's due for maintenance before the contacts coke up. I only want a crew sent if both the maintenance record and the oil support it.

Build these findings in order:

1. **Last tap changer job.** Pull the closed work orders on Transformer 1 and find the most recent one covering tap changer or OLTC work. Give me its number, description, completion date and failure code. Tell me how many days before 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 it was closed. If there has never been one, say so.

2. **Gas forecast.** Using the samples between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, check ethylene and hydrogen for gaps. Forecast both 3 days ahead, one step per day, with an 80% upper bound. Tell me whether either upper bound crosses its IEEE C57.104 Condition 1 limit on any day. The limits are 50 ppm for ethylene and 100 ppm for hydrogen.

3. **Fault class and supporting checks.** Run a dissolved gas fault classification on the latest complete sample using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene. Also give me:
   - the change in co from the first to the last sample, as a percentage
   - the phase current imbalance at the latest sample: the largest deviation of il1, il2 or il3 from their average, in percent, with inut alongside

The maintenance signal is met if no tap changer job was closed in the 365 days before 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000. The condition signal is met if the class is T2, T3 or D1, or if either forecast upper bound crosses its limit.

Decide as follows:
- **Both signals met.** First check open and pending-approval work orders on Transformer 1 for existing OLTC or tap changer work. If one exists, give me its number and don't duplicate it. Otherwise:
  - Create an OLTC inspection work order, coded with the closest tap changer failure code from our catalog.
  - Make it priority 1 if acetylene in the latest sample is above 1 ppm, and priority 2 otherwise.
  - Assign it to a technician who has done tap changer work on Transformer 1 before. If there is no such technician, use one who has worked on the unit before.
  - Start it on the first day in the next 14 days on which MAIN has fewer than 3 scheduled work orders.
- **Only one signal met.** Create nothing. Recommend a separate oil sample from the OLTC compartment, and tell me which signal wasn't met.
- **Paper involvement.** If co rose by more than 20% over the window, warn me that the heating may be in the core or winding with paper involved rather than in the tap changer. Say this whatever else you decide.

If ethylene or hydrogen has fewer than 4 usable samples, don't model it. Project its last value forward using the average daily change, and label it as a linear extrapolation with no interval. If our catalog has no tap changer failure code, leave the work order uncoded and say so.

# OLTC Wear Assessment — Transformer 1, MAIN (as of 2024-01-19)

## 1. Last tap changer job

**No tap changer work order has ever been closed on Transformer 1.** The only closed work order on this asset is:

- **WO 1000052** — "Transformer 1 oil sample retest and insulation check - DGA thermal fault (Rogers 1-0-2, T3 hot metal"
- Failure code: FC006
- Status: COMP, completed **2026-09-30** (after the 2024-01-19 reference date)

There is no completed tap changer/OLTC job, so the "days since last tap changer closure" metric does not apply — effectively it's been **far more than 365 days** since any OLTC work was closed (none ever).

**Maintenance signal: MET** (no tap changer job closed in the 365 days before 2024-01-19).

## 2. Gas forecast (2024-01-15 to 2024-01-19)

Both ethylene and hydrogen have exactly 4 usable samples in the window — no gaps. I cannot run a TSFM forecast (the forecasting toolchain is unavailable), so per your instruction I projected each gas forward 3 days using its average daily change. This is a **linear extrapolation with no confidence interval**:

| Day | Ethylene (ppm) | Hydrogen (ppm) |
|---|---|---|
| Last actual (Jan 18) | 16,600 | 2,900 |
| Jan 19 | 16,605.3 | 2,868.3 |
| Jan 20 | 16,610.7 | 2,836.7 |
| Jan 21 | 16,616.0 | 2,805.0 |

**Upper bounds:** Since no interval was available, I treat the extrapolation itself as the bound. **Both gases already far exceed their IEEE C57.104 Condition 1 limits** (ethylene 16,600 ppm vs 50 ppm limit; hydrogen 2,900 ppm vs 100 ppm limit) — they crossed long before this window and remain far above on every projected day. Condition limit crossings: **yes, both, on every day.**

**Condition signal contribution: MET** (forecast exceeds limits).

## 3. Fault classification and supporting checks

DGA Rogers/IEC classification could not be run (the interpretation tool's LLM backend is unavailable). Computing the Rogers ratios manually from the latest complete sample (2024-01-18: H2 2900, CH4 7350, C2H6 5450, C2H4 16600, C2H2 7):

- r1 = CH4/H2 = 7350/2900 = **2.53**
- r2 = C2H4/C2H6 = 16600/5450 = **3.04**
- r3 = C2H2/C2H4 = 7/16600 = **0.0004**

Ratios r1∈(1,3), r2>3, r3<0.1 → **T3 — thermal fault in oil, >700°C (hot metal)**. (Note: the closed WO 1000052 independently confirms this same Rogers 1-0-2 / T3 result for both the 01-15 and 01-18 samples.)

**Condition signal: MET** (class T3).

Supporting checks:
- **CO change:** 32 ppm (Jan 15) → 33 ppm (Jan 18) = **+3.1%** over the window.
- **Phase current imbalance (Jan 18):** il1=100, il2=106, il3=95; average = 100.33 A. Largest deviation is il3 at 5.33 A = **5.3%** imbalance, with **inut = 5 A**.

## Decision

**Both signals met.**

Checking for existing open/pending OLTC work: **WO 1000051** — "OLTC inspection - Transformer 1 on-load tap changer (suspected contact wear/coking)" — is already **APPR** on Transformer 1, priority 1, work type PdM, uncoded (no tap-changer failure code exists in the FCC catalog — the closest code, FC006 "overheating or high temperature reading," is generic, and the prior WO's notes already documented that no specific tap-changer code exists).

**No new work order created — WO 1000051 already covers this exact OLTC inspection and should not be duplicated.**

## Paper involvement

CO rose only 3.1% (32 → 33 ppm), well under the 20% threshold — **no paper-involvement warning is warranted.** The fault signature (T3 hot metal, negligible acetylene trend, minimal CO growth) is consistent with severe overheating in oil, not active carbon monoxide generation from paper insulation in the core/winding.
